curriculum.subject: English Studies
curriculum.topic: Pre-Reading Skills: Phonemic Awareness (Identifying Sounds)
curriculum.subtopic: Letter-Sound Identification (/a/, /b/, /c/, /d/) & Sound Production
curriculum.periodTitle: Instructional Week 1 · Foundational Phonics & Letter Sounds
objectives: Listen carefully and distinguish between different environmental and speech sounds
Pronounce the basic letter sounds /a/ as in apple, /b/ as in ball, /c/ as in cup
Identify objects in the classroom that begin with letter sounds /a/, /b/, /c/
Segment simple two-sound words like "at", "an", and "in"
curriculum.lastWeekRevision: Welcome to Primary 1! This is our very first week of learning how spoken words are built from tiny sounds.
curriculum.previousKnowledge: Pupils can recognize common everyday spoken words and imitate animal or vehicle sounds playfully.

concreteVisualAids.title: Letter Sound Flashcards
concreteVisualAids.description: Large colorful cards showing letters A, B, C with an apple, a ball, and a cup.
concreteVisualAids.caption: Phonics Sound Cards

concreteVisualAids.title: Classroom Sound Box
concreteVisualAids.description: A box of small toys: a bell, a ball, an orange, and a toy car to test sound identification.
concreteVisualAids.caption: Sound Discovery Box

whiteboardSteps.title: 1. What is a Letter Sound?
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Sannu kowa! In Primary 1, we learn that letters have names and letters make special sounds. When we say the letter "A", its sound is /æ/ like in "Amina" or "Apple"!
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
LETTER SOUNDS (PHONEMIC AWARENESS)

• Letter A says /æ/ → as in Apple 🍎, Ant 🐜
• Letter B says /b/ → as in Ball ⚽, Book 📖
• Letter C says /k/ → as in Cup ☕, Cat 🐱
bulletPoints: Every letter makes a sound with our mouth
We use our listening ears to hear the beginning sound
We say the sound clearly together!

whiteboardSteps.title: 2. Clapping Out the Sounds
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Let us clap whenever we hear the /b/ sound. Listen: "Ball!" (Clap!). "Banana!" (Clap!). "Book!" (Clap!). Excellent listening, champions!
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
LISTENING & BLENDING

• /b/ + /æ/ + /t/ = BAT 🏏
• /k/ + /æ/ + /t/ = CAT 🐱
• /æ/ + /t/ = AT
bulletPoints: Listen to each individual sound
Put the sounds together smoothly to make a word

practiceProblems.question: Which word starts with the /b/ sound like "Ball"?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Say each word slowly and listen to your lips at the start.
practiceProblems.explanation: "Book" starts with the /b/ sound, just like "Ball"!

practiceProblems.question: What sound does the letter "A" make in "Apple"?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Open your mouth wide like you are about to bite a sweet fruit.
practiceProblems.explanation: Letter A makes the /æ/ sound in apple and ant.

assessmentQuestions.question: Which of these fruits starts with the /a/ sound?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Look at the fruits in the market tray.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Apple begins with the /a/ sound: /æ/ - pple!
assessmentQuestions.hint: It is a red or green round fruit that starts with A.

assessmentQuestions.question: Amina sees a Cup on the table. What sound does the word "Cup" begin with?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Listen to the first sound: /k/ - up.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: "Cup" begins with the /k/ sound made by the letter C.
assessmentQuestions.hint: Make the sound at the back of your throat.

assessmentQuestions.question: Which word has the beginning sound /b/?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: What do children kick on the school field during break time?
assessmentQuestions.explanation: "Ball" begins with the letter B and the sound /b/.
assessmentQuestions.hint: It is round and bounces on the playground.

learningActivities: Direct teacher demonstration
Guided practice with concrete visual aids

curriculum.subject: Mathematics
curriculum.topic: Whole Numbers 1–5
curriculum.subtopic: Counting, Identification, and Writing Numbers 1 to 5
curriculum.periodTitle: Instructional Week 1 · Counting Objects 1 to 5 & Number Recognition
objectives: Count real concrete objects from 1 up to 5 accurately
Recognize and name the numerals 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Match a group of objects with its correct numeral
Trace and write numerals 1 to 5 with correct pencil strokes
curriculum.lastWeekRevision: Welcome to Primary 1 Mathematics! We are learning to count things around us.
curriculum.previousKnowledge: Children can show their fingers and know when they have one sweet or two sweets.

concreteVisualAids.title: Counting Oranges
concreteVisualAids.description: Five fresh, ripe Nigerian oranges lined up on a wooden table.
concreteVisualAids.caption: Counting 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 Oranges

concreteVisualAids.title: Counting Fingers Hand Chart
concreteVisualAids.description: A colorful chart showing 1 finger, 2 fingers, up to 5 fingers on one hand.
concreteVisualAids.caption: One Hand = 5 Fingers

whiteboardSteps.title: 1. Counting Objects 1 to 5
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Look at the oranges on our table. Let us count them together one by one: 1 orange, 2 oranges, 3 oranges, 4 oranges, 5 oranges! On one hand, we have exactly five fingers!
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
COUNTING WHOLE NUMBERS 1 TO 5

1 🍊 (One orange)
2 🍊🍊 (Two oranges)
3 🍊🍊🍊 (Three oranges)
4 🍊🍊🍊🍊 (Four oranges)
5 🍊🍊🍊🍊🍊 (Five oranges)
bulletPoints: Point to each object as you count
Say the number loud and proud
The last number you say is the total amount

whiteboardSteps.title: 2. Writing the Numerals
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Number 1 is like a straight standing stick: down we go and that is one! Number 2 is around and back on the railway track: two, two, two!
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
HOW TO WRITE 1 TO 5

1 : One straight line down
2 : Curve around and flat across the bottom
3 : Around a tree, around a tree
4 : Down and over, down once more
5 : Short neck, belly fat, number 5 wears a hat!
bulletPoints: Practice tracing with your finger in the air
Count the dots to check your answer

practiceProblems.question: Count the stars: ⭐ ⭐ ⭐. How many stars are there?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Touch each star with your finger as you count.
practiceProblems.explanation: Counting: 1, 2, 3! There are 3 stars.

practiceProblems.question: How many fingers are on one whole hand?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Hold up one hand and count your fingers.
practiceProblems.explanation: There are 5 fingers on one hand: thumb, index, middle, ring, and pinky!

assessmentQuestions.question: Chinedu has 4 ripe bananas in his bag. Which numeral shows 4?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Look closely at the numbers.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: The numeral 4 represents four items.
assessmentQuestions.hint: It is the number right after 3.

assessmentQuestions.question: Which group has exactly 2 objects?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Count the items in each choice.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: ⚽⚽ has two balls.
assessmentQuestions.hint: Look for a pair of footballs.

assessmentQuestions.question: What number comes immediately after 4 when counting forward?
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Counting forward: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The number after 4 is 5.
assessmentQuestions.hint: Count the fingers on one hand.

learningActivities: Direct teacher demonstration
Guided practice with concrete visual aids

curriculum.subject: Basic Science & Technology
curriculum.topic: Exploring Our Environment (Part 1)
curriculum.subtopic: Understanding what an environment is, identifying our surroundings, and using our senses
curriculum.periodTitle: Instructional Week 1 · What is Our Environment? Exploring With Our Senses
objectives: Define our environment as everything around us in our home, school, and community
Name common things found in our immediate classroom and school surroundings
Identify how we use our five senses (seeing, hearing, smelling, touching, tasting) to explore our surroundings safely
Differentiate between natural things (trees, grass, sun) and man-made things (desks, pencils, blackboard)
curriculum.lastWeekRevision: Welcome to your very first Basic Science lesson in Primary 1! Today we become young scientists who observe the world.
curriculum.previousKnowledge: Pupils know their way to school and can recognize trees, classroom chairs, books, and playground sand.

concreteVisualAids.caption: We Explore with Our 5 Senses

whiteboardSteps.title: 1. What is an Environment?
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Sannu my young scientists! An environment is everything that surrounds us. Wherever you are right now—look up at the ceiling, look down at the floor, look at your desk, look at your teacher—all of that is your environment! At home, your bedroom and compound are your home environment. In school, our compound and classrooms are our school environment.
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
WHAT IS OUR ENVIRONMENT?

• Environment = Everything around us!
• Examples in our Classroom:
  - Wooden desks and chairs 🪑
  - Blackboard and white chalk 🖍️
  - Books and school bags 🎒
  - Our teacher and school friends 🧑‍🤝‍🧑
bulletPoints: Our environment is everywhere we go
We must keep our environment clean and tidy
Things in our environment can be living or non-living

whiteboardSteps.title: 2. Exploring with Our Five Senses
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: How do we know what is in our environment? God gave us five wonderful senses! We use our EYES to see colors and shapes. We use our EARS to hear the teacher’s voice and the birds singing outside. We use our NOSE to smell flowers. We use our HANDS and skin to feel smooth paper or rough tree bark. But remember: we never taste unknown things in the classroom!
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
OUR 5 SENSES FOR EXPLORING

1. 👀 Eyes → Seeing (trees, colors, books)
2. 👂 Ears → Hearing (school bell, birds, songs)
3. 👃 Nose → Smelling (fresh rain, flowers)
4. ✋ Skin/Hands → Touching (smooth table, rough bark)
5. 👅 Tongue → Tasting (sweet orange, warm pap)
bulletPoints: Always use your eyes and ears to explore first
Touch gently without breaking things
Never put strange objects into your mouth

practiceProblems.question: Which of our five senses do we use to see the green leaves on a mango tree?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Point to the part of your face that helps you see pictures.
practiceProblems.explanation: We use our eyes to see colors, people, and things around us in our environment.

practiceProblems.question: Which of these is something we see inside our classroom environment?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Look at what you sit on during your lessons.
practiceProblems.explanation: A classroom desk is part of our school and classroom environment.

assessmentQuestions.question: What is the meaning of "environment"?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Remember what Mallama Zainab taught us today.
options: Only the toys in our room
Everything around us in our home, school, and community
Only big animals in the forest
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Our environment means everything that surrounds us wherever we are.
assessmentQuestions.hint: It includes everything you can see, hear, and touch around you.

assessmentQuestions.question: When the school bell rings for break time, which sense do you use to hear it?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Ding! Dong! The bell is ringing!
assessmentQuestions.explanation: We use our ears to hear sounds like the school bell, singing, and speech.
assessmentQuestions.hint: You have two of them on the sides of your head.

assessmentQuestions.question: Which of these things in our school environment was made by nature, not by a carpenter?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Look outside in the school compound.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: A green mango tree is a living plant from nature; desks and rulers are made by human beings.
assessmentQuestions.hint: It grows from the ground and has fresh green leaves.

whiteboardSteps.title: 1. Naming Our Body Parts
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Good day active champions! Stand up straight and let us play "Teacher Says"! Teacher says: touch your head! Good! Teacher says: touch your two shoulders! Wonderful! Now wiggle your ten fingers in the air like stars! Our bodies have three main sections: head at the top, trunk in the middle, and limbs (arms and legs) that help us move.
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
OUR BODY PARTS

• Top: Head, neck, eyes, ears 🗣️
• Middle: Shoulders, chest, waist 👕
• Limbs:
  - Arms, elbows, hands, fingers (Upper Limbs) ✋
  - Thighs, knees, legs, feet, toes (Lower Limbs) 🦵
bulletPoints: Every body part has a special job
Hands help us write, eat, and clap
Legs and feet help us walk, march, and jump

whiteboardSteps.title: 2. Safe and Healthy Body Movements
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Let us practice moving each part without bumping into our neighbors. Gently nod your head up and down: "Yes, yes, yes". Slowly turn your head left and right: "No, no, no". Shrug your shoulders up to your ears and let them drop! Now march on the spot: one-two, one-two! Moving every day keeps our blood flowing and our minds sharp.
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
SAFE WARM-UP MOVEMENTS

1. Head Nodding: Up and down gently
2. Shoulder Rolls: Backward and forward
3. Arm Reaches: Stretch high to touch the clouds!
4. Knee Bends: Gentle bend and stand tall
5. Spot Marching: Lift knees high, 1-2, 1-2!
bulletPoints: Keep your space: do not bump into classmates
Breathe in fresh air through your nose, out through your mouth
Drink clean water after exercising

practiceProblems.question: Which body parts do you use to kick a football across the field?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Think about playing on the playground during games time.
practiceProblems.explanation: We use our legs and feet to kick a ball, run, and jump.

practiceProblems.question: When we nod our head up and down, what does that movement usually mean?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Do it right now: nod up and down gently.
practiceProblems.explanation: Nodding the head up and down is a polite movement that usually means "Yes".

assessmentQuestions.question: Which of the following body parts is located on your upper body between your neck and your arms?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Place your hands right here on your body.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Our shoulders connect our neck to our arms on our upper body.
assessmentQuestions.hint: In the song: "Head, shoulders, knees and toes!"

assessmentQuestions.question: Why is it important to do simple stretching exercises every morning before learning?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Think about how you feel after morning assembly.
options: To make us feel sleepy and tired
To keep our bodies active, flexible, and healthy
So we cannot write with our pencils
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Stretching and exercising keeps our muscles flexible and our minds awake and alert.
assessmentQuestions.hint: It gives us energy and keeps our bodies strong.

assessmentQuestions.question: How many toes do we have on our two feet combined?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Count 5 toes on your left foot and 5 toes on your right foot.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: We have 5 toes on each foot, making a total of 10 toes.
assessmentQuestions.hint: Just like we have 10 fingers on our two hands.

curriculum.subject: Christian Religious Studies
curriculum.topic: God the Creator (Part 1)
curriculum.subtopic: God is the Supreme Creator who made the universe, Day 1 (Light & Darkness), and Day 2 (Sky & Clouds)
curriculum.periodTitle: Instructional Week 1 · God Made Our Beautiful World (Day 1 & Day 2)
objectives: Identify God as the Supreme Being and Loving Creator of the world
Explain the creation of Day 1: God said "Let there be light", separating light (Day) from darkness (Night)
Explain the creation of Day 2: God created the firmament, forming the beautiful sky and clouds
Appreciate God’s love and wisdom in giving us day for work and night for restful sleep
curriculum.lastWeekRevision: Welcome to Primary 1 Christian Religious Studies! We begin with the greatest story of all: how God created everything.
curriculum.previousKnowledge: Pupils know that night is dark when they sleep, and morning brings bright sunlight for going to school.

concreteVisualAids.title: Day 1 Creation Picture (Light and Night)
concreteVisualAids.description: Vivid illustration split in half: one side has bright sunshine and blue sky, the other has a glowing moon and stars.
concreteVisualAids.caption: Day 1: God Created Light

concreteVisualAids.title: Day 2 Creation Picture (The Sky Above)
concreteVisualAids.description: Peaceful picture of puffy white clouds and endless blue sky spanning above the earth.
concreteVisualAids.caption: Day 2: God Formed the Sky

whiteboardSteps.title: 1. God is the Supreme Creator
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Welcome, dear scholars! Before there were trees, before there were houses, roads, or people, only God existed. God is the Almighty Supreme Being. God looked upon darkness and decided to create a magnificent world full of wonder for us to live in and enjoy.
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
GOD THE CREATOR

• God is the Supreme Being
• God has no beginning and no end
• God created the world out of love
• Everything God made is good and beautiful!
bulletPoints: God spoke and creation came to be
God cares for every child and every creature
We say "Thank You God" for life and light
whiteboardSteps.equationOrHighlight: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.

whiteboardSteps.title: 2. Day 1 and Day 2 of Creation
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: On the very first day, the world was completely dark. God spoke with authority: "Let there be light!" And immediately, bright light appeared! God separated the light from the darkness. He called the light DAY, and the darkness NIGHT. On the second day, God formed the great expanse of the sky to divide the waters above and below. Look up outside—the beautiful blue sky with soft white clouds was made on Day 2!
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
THE FIRST TWO DAYS OF CREATION

• DAY 1: Light and Darkness
  - Light = DAY ☀️ (Time to learn, play, and work)
  - Darkness = NIGHT 🌙 (Time to rest and sleep)

• DAY 2: The Sky and Clouds ☁️
  - God created the dome of the sky
  - The sky protects our earth and gives us air to breathe
bulletPoints: Day 1 gave us day and night
Day 2 gave us the expansive sky
God saw that it was good!
whiteboardSteps.equationOrHighlight: Day 1: Light & Night | Day 2: Sky & Clouds

practiceProblems.question: What did God create on the very first day of creation when He said "Let there be light"?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Think of what shines into your bedroom in the morning.
practiceProblems.explanation: On Day 1, God created light and separated it from darkness, creating Day and Night.

practiceProblems.question: What did God name the time of light?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: What do we call the hours when the sun is up and you are at school?
practiceProblems.explanation: God called the light Day, and He called the darkness Night.

assessmentQuestions.question: Who is the Supreme Creator who made the heavens, the earth, and everything in them?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Remember the opening verse of the Holy Bible.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: God Almighty is the Supreme Being and Creator of the universe.
assessmentQuestions.hint: He spoke and the world was formed.

assessmentQuestions.question: What did God create on Day 2 of creation that we see when we look up outside?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Look up above the school roof into the open air.
options: The beautiful blue sky and clouds
assessmentQuestions.explanation: On Day 2, God created the sky (firmament) with its clouds.
assessmentQuestions.hint: It is high above our heads, blue in color with white puffy clouds.

assessmentQuestions.question: Why did God give us the darkness of night time?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: What do you and your family do when darkness falls and the stars come out?
options: So we can play football in the dark
For rest, peace, and healthy sleep
So we cannot see our food
Because God ran out of colors
assessmentQuestions.explanation: God in His wisdom gave us the night so our bodies and minds can rest and sleep peacefully.
assessmentQuestions.hint: It is when we lie down on our bed to recharge for the next day.

objectives: Recognize and pronounce the first seven Arabic letters: Alif (أ), Baa (ب), Taa (ت), Thaa (ث), Jeem (ج), Haa (ح), Khaa (خ)

Count and locate the dots (Nuqat) that differentiate Baa (1 dot below), Taa (2 dots above), and Thaa (3 dots above)

whiteboardSteps.title: 1. Reading Right to Left & Letter Alif (أ)
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Assalamu Alaikum, my lovely scholars! In Arabic, we read from right to left! Look at our first letter: ALIF (أ). It stands tall and straight like a walking stick or a tall pencil. When we say Alif, we open our mouth gently. Say it with me: "ALIF!"
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
THE ARABIC ALPHABET (READ RIGHT TO LEFT ➡️ ⬅️)

1. أ (Alif) → Straight line from top to bottom
• Sound: Clear open sound like /a/
• Looks like: A standing staff or pencil ✏️
bulletPoints: Arabic is read from RIGHT to LEFT
Alif is the very first letter
Alif has no dots

whiteboardSteps.title: 2. The Boat Family and The Curved Family
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Now meet the Boat Family: Baa (ب), Taa (ت), and Thaa (ث). They all have the same boat shape, but notice the dots! Baa has ONE dot underneath (like a fish swimming under the boat). Taa has TWO dots inside at the top (like two friendly eyes). Thaa has THREE dots at the top! Next come the curved letters: Jeem (ج) has a dot in its tummy, Haa (ح) has no dot, and Khaa (خ) has a dot sitting on its head!
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
DOTS MAKE THE DIFFERENCE!

• THE BOAT FAMILY:
  - ب (Baa) → 1 dot BELOW
  - ت (Taa) → 2 dots ABOVE
  - ث (Thaa) → 3 dots ABOVE

• THE CURVED FAMILY:
  - ج (Jeem) → 1 dot in the tummy
  - ح (Haa) → Clean! No dot at all
  - خ (Khaa) → 1 dot on top of the head
bulletPoints: Count the dots to know the letter
ب has one dot under the line
ت has two dots on top
ج, ح, خ share the same curved tail
whiteboardSteps.equationOrHighlight: أ • ب • ت • ث • ج • ح • خ

practiceProblems.question: Which Arabic letter has ONE single dot underneath its boat shape?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Think of the letter with the dot below like a fish under water: ب.
practiceProblems.explanation: Baa (ب) has one single dot placed directly below the letter shape.

practiceProblems.question: In which direction do we read and write Arabic text?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Remember: start on the side of your right hand!
practiceProblems.explanation: Arabic is written and read from right to left.

assessmentQuestions.question: What is the very first letter of the Arabic alphabet?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: It stands straight and tall with no dots.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Alif (أ) is the first letter of the Arabic alphabet.
assessmentQuestions.hint: It looks like a straight standing vertical line.

assessmentQuestions.question: How many dots does the letter Taa (ت) have on top?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Look at the two eyes sitting inside the boat: ت.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Taa (ت) has exactly two dots placed above the boat line.
assessmentQuestions.hint: Count the dots: one, two!

assessmentQuestions.question: Among the curved letters ج, ح, and خ, which one has NO dots at all?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Look at the clean, smooth letter: ح.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Haa (ح) is written completely clean without any dots.
assessmentQuestions.hint: Jeem has a dot in its tummy and Khaa has a dot on its head.

whiteboardSteps.title: 1. What is History?
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Hello future leaders! Have you ever listened to your grandmother tell you a story by the fireside or in the living room? History is the true story of things that happened in the past. It is not an imaginary cartoon or a made-up movie. History tells us the real truth about what happened yesterday, last month, fifty years ago, or hundreds of years ago in our homeland, Nigeria!
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
WHAT IS HISTORY?

• History = The true story of the past!
• "The Past" means time that has already gone by:
  - Yesterday when you ate dinner 🍲
  - When you were a tiny crawling baby 👶
  - When your parents went to school 🎒
  - When Nigeria was young 🇳🇬
bulletPoints: History tells real stories of real people
History explains how we got to where we are today
Knowing our past makes us proud and wise
whiteboardSteps.equationOrHighlight: History = True Story of the Past

whiteboardSteps.title: 2. Why Do We Study History?
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Why do we study history? First, history helps us know our family. When your parents tell you about your village, your town, and your great-grandparents, you learn your roots! Second, history teaches us lessons from brave heroes who built our schools, hospitals, and towns. By learning about good deeds in the past, we learn how to be good citizens today.
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
WHY WE STUDY HISTORY

1. To Know Our Roots: Where our family and town came from
2. To Learn from the Past: What worked well and what mistakes to avoid
3. To Celebrate Our Heroes: Men and women who built our nation
4. To Love Our Country: Knowing Nigeria’s rich culture and heritage
bulletPoints: Every Nigerian community has a rich history
We listen carefully to stories told by our elders
We keep old family photographs and memories safe
whiteboardSteps.equationOrHighlight: Learn from Yesterday · Live Well Today · Lead Tomorrow

practiceProblems.question: Which of the following describes what "History" is?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Remember what Mallama Zainab explained about real stories.
options: The true story of events and people in the past
A game played with football on the field
A recipe for cooking jollof rice
practiceProblems.explanation: History is the true record and story of what really happened in the past.

practiceProblems.question: Which of these events belongs to your own personal past history?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Think of something that already happened before today.
options: What you will eat tomorrow morning
The day you took your first steps as a baby
Your graduation from university in 15 years
practiceProblems.explanation: The day you took your first steps as a baby already happened in the past, so it is part of your history.

assessmentQuestions.question: What word do we use for the time that has already happened, like yesterday or last year?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Is it the future, or is it the past?
assessmentQuestions.explanation: The past refers to all the days and years that have already passed by.
assessmentQuestions.hint: It is behind us in time, like yesterday.

assessmentQuestions.question: Who can tell us true stories about what our family and hometown were like long ago?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Think of the respected elders in your family.
options: A baby who cannot speak yet
A strange stranger in the street
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Our parents and grandparents have lived through many years and can tell us our family history.
assessmentQuestions.hint: They have grey hair and remember when our parents were small.

assessmentQuestions.question: Why is it good for Nigerian children to study the history of our country?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Think about how learning about Nigeria makes us proud citizens.
options: So we can forget our family names
To learn good lessons, know our culture, and love our homeland
So we do not have to do our school homework
To argue with our school teachers
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Learning history helps us understand our rich culture, learn from the past, and grow into great leaders.
assessmentQuestions.hint: It helps us know how our nation became great.

whiteboardSteps.title: 1. What is a Leader?
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Welcome, young citizens! A leader is someone who shows the way, guides others, and takes care of a group so that everyone is safe, happy, and successful. When a flock of birds flies in the sky, one bird leads the way. In our classroom, when we walk to the library, the line leader walks gently in front so no one gets lost!
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
WHAT IS A LEADER?

• A Leader = Someone who guides, directs, and helps others.
• Leaders in Our Lives:
  - At HOME 🏠: Our Mother and Father (Parents)
  - In CLASSROOM 🏫: Our Teacher
  - In SCHOOL 🏢: The Headteacher / Principal
  - In COMMUNITY 🏘️: Village Head, Oba, Emir, or Eze
bulletPoints: A good leader serves and protects the group
Without leaders, there would be confusion and quarreling
Good leaders listen to those they lead
whiteboardSteps.equationOrHighlight: A Leader Guides with Wisdom and Love

whiteboardSteps.title: 2. Qualities of a Good Leader
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: What makes someone a truly great leader? A good leader is NOT a bully who shouts or takes other children’s pencils. No! A good leader is KIND to everyone, HONEST by always telling the truth, FAIR by sharing treats equally, and HELPFUL when someone falls or struggles with classwork. You too can be a great leader in Primary 1!
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
QUALITIES OF A GOOD LEADER

1. ❤️ KINDNESS: Treats everyone with respect and care
2. 🤝 HONESTY: Always tells the truth and keeps promises
3. ⚖️ FAIRNESS: Treats all children equally without favoritism
4. 🤲 HELPFULNESS: Assists those who need support
bulletPoints: A leader leads by good example
We greet and respect our leaders politely
Every child in Primary 1 can practice being a leader

practiceProblems.question: Who is the primary leader that guides and teaches pupils inside our classroom every day?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Look at the teacher standing at the whiteboard.
practiceProblems.explanation: The class teacher is the leader who guides pupils and teaches lessons in the classroom.

practiceProblems.question: Which of the following actions shows that a class captain is a GOOD leader?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Think about kindness and fairness.
options: Taking other children’s snacks without asking
Helping a classmate who dropped their pencils pick them up
Shouting loudly during quiet reading time
practiceProblems.explanation: Helping a friend pick up fallen pencils shows kindness and helpful leadership.

assessmentQuestions.question: Who are the leaders God gave you to protect and care for you inside your home?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Think of who provides your food, clothes, and shelter at home.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Parents are the God-given leaders of the home who love, guide, and protect their children.
assessmentQuestions.hint: They wake you up, prepare your breakfast, and pray for you.

assessmentQuestions.question: Which of these is a very important quality of a good leader?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Look at the qualities of a trustworthy person.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Honesty is a core quality of a good leader because people must trust their leader.
assessmentQuestions.hint: It means speaking the truth at all times.

assessmentQuestions.question: Why do we need a headteacher in our primary school?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Think about who oversees the entire school compound.
options: To eat all the school biscuits
To keep the school organized, safe, and peaceful for learning
To hide the books from children
So teachers do not come to school
assessmentQuestions.explanation: The headteacher manages the teachers and pupils so the whole school is safe and orderly.
assessmentQuestions.hint: They ensure everything runs smoothly from morning assembly to dismissal.

whiteboardSteps.title: 1. What is Art?
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Hello creative artists! Look at your clothes, look at the colorful illustrations in your reading book, look at the bright flags in the school yard. All of that was designed through ART! Art is the wonderful way we use our imagination, our hearts, and our hands to create beautiful things that bring joy to others.
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
WHAT IS ART?

• Art = Creating beautiful things with our imagination and hands! 🎨
• Forms of Art in Primary 1:
  - ✏️ Drawing: Making lines and shapes with pencils
  - 🖍️ Coloring: Filling shapes with bright crayons
  - 🖌️ Painting: Spreading colors with a soft brush
  - ✂️ Paper Craft: Folding and pasting clean paper shapes
bulletPoints: Art helps us express our thoughts and feelings
Everyone can create art in their own unique way
Art makes our classrooms and homes beautiful

whiteboardSteps.title: 2. Art Tools and Caring for Our Materials
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: To make art, artists need tools! In our classroom, our most important tools are clean white paper, a sharp HB pencil, and colorful wax crayons. When using your crayons, hold them gently near the tip so they do not snap. And remember our golden rule: we color only on our paper sketchpads, NEVER on classroom walls or desks!
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
OUR ART TOOLS & CARE RULES

• Common Art Materials:
  1. Plain drawing paper or sketchpad 📄
  2. Lead pencil & soft eraser ✏️
  3. Wax crayons & colored pencils 🖍️

• GOLDEN RULES OF THE ART CLASS:
  ✅ Color inside your drawing book
  ✅ Put crayons back in their box after use
  ❌ Do not write or draw on walls or desks
bulletPoints: Take care of your art materials so they last all term
Share colors politely with your desk partner
Always wash your hands after art class
whiteboardSteps.equationOrHighlight: Color on Paper · Care for Your Tools

practiceProblems.question: Which of these materials do we use in our classroom to add bright colors to our drawings?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Look inside your pencil case for the colorful sticks.
practiceProblems.explanation: Wax crayons are used to color pictures with bright colors like red, yellow, and blue.

practiceProblems.question: Where should a good Primary 1 pupil draw their art pictures?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Remember Mallama Zainab’s golden rule for art.
practiceProblems.explanation: We always draw and color inside our drawing sketchpad or on clean paper, never on walls or furniture.

assessmentQuestions.question: What is art?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Think about making something lovely with your hands.
options: Creating beautiful things with our imagination and hands
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Art is the joyful creation of beautiful things using our minds and hands.
assessmentQuestions.hint: It brings beauty and happiness to our eyes.

assessmentQuestions.question: Which of the following is a tool used for drawing the initial outline of a picture?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: You use this to draw lines before coloring them in.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: A pencil is used by artists to draw outlines, shapes, and figures.
assessmentQuestions.hint: It has graphite inside and makes a grey line on paper.

assessmentQuestions.question: After finishing your drawing, what is the right thing to do with your crayons and pencils?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Think of keeping your desk neat and tidy.
options: Throw them on the classroom floor
Pack them neatly back into your pencil pouch or box
Break them in half and give them away
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Caring for art tools means packing them neatly into their box so they remain clean and ready for next time.
assessmentQuestions.hint: Put them away safely so they do not get stepped on or lost.

whiteboardSteps.title: 1. Grouping in Tens and Units
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Welcome to Primary 2! Today we count up to 100. Look at these sticks. Instead of counting single sticks all day, we tie 10 sticks together into a bundle. One bundle is called 1 TEN. If we have 3 bundles and 4 loose sticks, we have 3 Tens and 4 Units = 34!
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
PLACE VALUE: TENS (T) & UNITS (U)

• Number 34:
  3 Tens = 30
  4 Units = 4
  30 + 4 = 34 (Thirty-four)

• Number 50:
  5 Tens = 50
  0 Units = 0
bulletPoints: Units = Single loose objects (0 to 9)
Tens = Bundles of 10 objects
10 Tens together make ONE HUNDRED (100)

whiteboardSteps.title: 2. Writing Numbers in Words
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Let us practice writing numbers in words. 10 is ten, 20 is twenty, 30 is thirty, 40 is forty, and 100 is one hundred!
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
NUMBERS IN WORDS

• 14 = Fourteen
• 40 = Forty (Notice: F-O-R-T-Y)
• 75 = Seventy-five
• 100 = One hundred
bulletPoints: Read the Tens first, then the Units
Always put a hyphen between tens and units: twenty-five, sixty-three

practiceProblems.question: In the number 57, what is the place value of the digit 5?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: 57 has 5 bundles of ten and 7 loose units.
practiceProblems.explanation: In 57, the digit 5 is in the Tens place (5 Tens = 50).

practiceProblems.question: How do you write the number 48 in words?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Say the tens part first, then the units.
practiceProblems.explanation: 48 is written as "Forty-eight".

assessmentQuestions.question: What is the value of 6 Tens and 3 Units?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Combine 6 bundles of ten sticks and 3 single sticks.
assessmentQuestions.hint: Put the 6 in the Tens column and 3 in the Units column.

assessmentQuestions.question: Which of the following numbers is the greatest?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Compare the tens digits first.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: 86 has 8 tens and 6 units, which is greater than 81, 79, and 68.
assessmentQuestions.hint: Both 86 and 81 have 8 tens. Which has more units?

assessmentQuestions.question: What number comes immediately after 99 when counting forward?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Think about when you add 1 more to 99.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: 99 + 1 = 100 (One Hundred).
assessmentQuestions.hint: It is a 3-digit number with two zeros.

objectives: What is a first aid box? Box with items for treating injuries

Contents of first aid box: - Bandages and plasters (for covering cuts) - Cotton wool (for cleaning wounds) - Antiseptic liquid/cream (for cleaning cuts) - Scissors (for cutting bandages) - Thermometer (for checking temperature) - Safety pins
Where to find first aid boxes: school clinic, home, car
Never play with first aid items
Activity: Identifying first aid items, creating class first aid poster

curriculum.topic: First Aid: Treating Minor Injuries (Part 1)
curriculum.subtopic: Treating small cuts and scrapes: 1. Tell an adult immediately 2. Clean with clean water 3. Apply antiseptic (adult does this) 4. Cover with plaster or bandage
objectives: Treating small cuts and scrapes: 1. Tell an adult immediately 2. Clean with clean water 3. Apply antiseptic (adult does this) 4. Cover with plaster or bandage
Treating bruises: - Apply cold compress (ice pack or cold cloth) - Rest the hurt part
What NOT to do: - Don't touch wound with dirty hands - Don't remove bandage too soon

curriculum.topic: First Aid: Treating Minor Injuries (Part 2)
curriculum.subtopic: Treating nose bleeding: - Sit upright, don't lie down - Lean forward slightly - Pinch soft part of nose - Breathe through mouth - Get adult help
objectives: Treating nose bleeding: - Sit upright, don't lie down - Lean forward slightly - Pinch soft part of nose - Breathe through mouth - Get adult help
Treating insect bites/stings: - Don't scratch - Wash with soap and water - Apply cream (adult does this) - Tell adult if swelling or pain
Treating minor burns (from hot water, sun): - Run cool water over burn - Don't apply ice directly - Cover with clean cloth - Get adult help immediately
Activity: First aid scenarios, what would you do?

objectives: Understanding roads: where vehicles move
Dangers on roads: moving cars, motorcycles, bicycles

Traffic lights: red (stop), yellow (get ready), green (go)
Activity: Road safety role-play, crossing practice (in safe area)

objectives: Stranger danger: - Don't talk to strangers - Don't follow strangers - Don't accept gifts from strangers - Don't go anywhere with strangers - Scream and run if stranger tries to take you

God listens when we pray
We can pray anywhere: home, school, church, playground

God loves it when we pray

curriculum.subject: Christian Religious Studies
curriculum.topic: Jesus' Power Over Natural Forces (Part 1): Jesus Calms the Storm
curriculum.subtopic: Story: Jesus and disciples in a boat on the sea (Mark 4:35-41)
objectives: Story: Jesus and disciples in a boat on the sea (Mark 4:35-41)
A big storm came: strong wind, big waves, boat filling with water
Disciples were afraid: "We are going to drown!"
Jesus was sleeping in the boat
They woke Jesus: "Teacher, don't you care that we are dying?"
Jesus stood up and said to the storm: "Peace! Be still!"
The wind stopped, the sea became calm
Jesus asked: "Why are you afraid? Do you have no faith?"
Lesson: Jesus has power over nature (wind and waves)
Activity: Acting out the story, drawing the scene, discussing what we learn

curriculum.subtopic: Story: Jesus walks on water (Matthew 14:22-33)
objectives: Story: Jesus walks on water (Matthew 14:22-33)
Disciples in boat at night, Jesus on land praying
Jesus walked on the water toward the boat
Disciples were frightened: "It's a ghost!"
Jesus said: "It is I. Don't be afraid."
Peter wanted to walk on water too
Peter walked on water but got scared and started to sink
Jesus saved Peter
Lesson: Jesus can do what is impossible for us; we must have faith
Activity: Retelling story, discussing miracles, water experiments (things that float/sink)

objectives: Story: Jesus feeds 5,000 people (John 6:1-14)
Many people followed Jesus to hear Him teach
It was late, people were hungry
A boy had 5 loaves of bread and 2 fish
Jesus took the food, prayed, and gave thanks to God
Jesus gave the food to disciples to share
Everyone ate and was satisfied
There were 12 baskets of leftovers!
Lesson: Jesus can multiply what we have; sharing is important
Activity: Counting exercise (5 loaves, 2 fish, 12 baskets), discussing sharing

curriculum.topic: Jesus' Power Over Death (Part 1): Jesus Raises Jairus' Daughter
curriculum.subtopic: Story: Jairus' daughter raised from the dead (Mark 5:21-43)
objectives: Story: Jairus' daughter raised from the dead (Mark 5:21-43)
Jairus was a synagogue leader, his daughter was very sick
He asked Jesus to come and heal her
While they were going, news came: "Your daughter is dead"
Jesus said: "Don't be afraid, just believe"
They went to the house, people were crying
Jesus said: "She is not dead, she is sleeping"
Jesus said: "Little girl, get up!" and she got up
Lesson: Jesus has power over death; nothing is impossible for Jesus
Activity: Storytelling with pictures, discussing Jesus' power

curriculum.subtopic: Story: Jesus raises Lazarus from the dead (John 11:1- (Part 2): Jesus Raises Lazarus 44)
objectives: Story: Jesus raises Lazarus from the dead (John 11:1- (Part 2): Jesus Raises Lazarus 44)
Lazarus was Jesus' friend, he was very sick
Lazarus died and was buried for four days
Jesus came to Bethany
Martha and Mary were sad
Jesus said: "I am the resurrection and the life"
Jesus went to the tomb and said: "Lazarus, come out!"
Lazarus came out, alive!
Lesson: Jesus gives life; Jesus cares about our sadness
Activity: Retelling story, discussing how Jesus comforts us

curriculum.topic: Abraham (Part 1): God's Promise to Abraham
curriculum.subtopic: Who was Abraham? A man who loved and obeyed God
objectives: Who was Abraham? A man who loved and obeyed God
Abraham lived in a place called Ur
God spoke to Abraham: "Leave your country and go to a land I will show you"
God's promises to Abraham: - "I will make you a great nation" - "I will bless you" - "You will be a blessing to others" - "I will give this land to your descendants"
Abraham obeyed God and left his home
Lesson: God makes promises and keeps them; we should obey God
Activity: Drawing Abraham's journey, map activity

curriculum.topic: Abraham (Part 2): The Birth of Isaac
curriculum.subtopic: Abraham and Sarah had no children, they were old
objectives: Abraham and Sarah had no children, they were old
God promised them a son
Sarah laughed because she was too old
But God said: "Nothing is impossible with God"
When Abraham was 100 years old, Isaac was born!
God kept His promise
Isaac means "laughter" - they were so happy
Lesson: God keeps His promises even when it seems impossible; God's timing is perfect
Activity: Discussing waiting for promises, celebrating with drawing/songs

curriculum.subject: Christian Religious Studies
curriculum.topic: Abraham (Part 3): God Tests Abraham's Faith
curriculum.subtopic: Story: Abraham and Isaac (Genesis 22:1-18 - age- appropriate version)
objectives: Story: Abraham and Isaac (Genesis 22:1-18 - age- appropriate version)
God tested Abraham's faith
God asked Abraham to offer Isaac
Abraham loved Isaac but he loved and trusted God more
Abraham obeyed and took Isaac to the mountain
When Abraham was about to obey, God stopped him
God provided a ram instead
God said: "Now I know you fear God"
God blessed Abraham for his obedience
Lesson: True faith means obeying God completely; God provides what we need
Activity: Discussing obedience, trust in God

curriculum.subtopic: Abraham's family grew into a large nation (Part 1): The Israelites in Egypt (Israelites)
objectives: Abraham's family grew into a large nation (Part 1): The Israelites in Egypt (Israelites)
They went to Egypt because of famine
At first, Egyptians were kind to them
Later, a new Pharaoh made them slaves
The Israelites worked hard: making bricks, building
They were treated badly
The Israelites cried to God for help
God heard their prayers and remembered His promise to Abraham
Lesson: God hears our prayers when we cry to Him
Activity: Discussing how God helps people in trouble, prayer time

curriculum.topic: Deliverance from Egypt (Part 2): Moses and the Burning Bush
curriculum.subtopic: God chose Moses to deliver the Israelites
objectives: God chose Moses to deliver the Israelites
Moses was keeping sheep in the wilderness
He saw a bush on fire but it didn't burn up
God spoke to Moses from the bush
God said: "I have seen my people suffering in Egypt"
"I am sending you to Pharaoh to bring my people out"
Moses was afraid but God promised to be with him
Lesson: God calls people to help others; God is always with us
Activity: Acting out the burning bush scene, discussing being brave

curriculum.topic: Deliverance from Egypt (Part 3): The Passover and Crossing the Red Sea
curriculum.subtopic: Moses went to Pharaoh: "Let my people go!"
objectives: Moses went to Pharaoh: "Let my people go!"
Pharaoh refused many times
God sent plagues (troubles) on Egypt
The last plague: Passover (God protected Israelites)
Finally, Pharaoh let them go
The Israelites left Egypt (the Exodus)
Pharaoh changed his mind and chased them
They reached the Red Sea - trapped!
Moses stretched his hand, God parted the sea
The Israelites walked through on dry ground
The Egyptian army was defeated
Lesson: God delivers His people; God is more powerful than any enemy
Activity: Creating Red Sea crossing scene, retelling with actions

curriculum.topic: Entry into the Promised
curriculum.subtopic: God led the Israelites through the wilderness Land (Part 1): Journey to Canaan
objectives: God led the Israelites through the wilderness Land (Part 1): Journey to Canaan
They were going to Canaan, the Promised Land
God provided for them: - Manna (bread from heaven) every morning - Quail (birds) for meat - Water from a rock - Cloud by day, fire by night (God's presence)
The journey was long (40 years) because of disobedience
Moses led them but Joshua took over later
Lesson: God provides for His people; obedience is important
Activity: Discussing God's provision, creating wilderness journey poster

curriculum.topic: Entry into the Promised Land (Part 2): Crossing the Jordan and Entering Canaan
curriculum.subtopic: Joshua became the new leader
objectives: Joshua became the new leader
God spoke to Joshua: "Be strong and courageous"
The Israelites reached the Jordan River
God made the water stop flowing
They walked across on dry ground (like the Red Sea)
They entered the Promised Land - Canaan!
God kept His promise to Abraham
Jerusalem became their special city later
Story: The walls of Jericho fell down (God's power)
Lesson: God always keeps His promises; be strong and trust God
Activity: Building and knocking down Jericho walls (blocks), celebrating God's faithfulness

Treating everyone fairly (social justice)

Rural (village) - farms, quiet, close to nature

Appreciating diversity in communities
How different communities help each other
Our role in making community better

curriculum.subject: Basic Science & Technology
curriculum.topic: Measurement of Length I
curriculum.subtopic: Meaning of Length, Traditional Units (Handspan, Arm length, Footsteps) and Metric Units
curriculum.periodTitle: Instructional Week 1 · Understanding Length & Measurement Methods
objectives: Define length as the distance between two points
Identify traditional non-standard methods of measuring length (handspan, footsteps, arm length, cubit)
Explain the limitations of traditional measurement methods
Introduce standard metric units of length: centimeters (cm) and meters (m)
curriculum.lastWeekRevision: Welcome to Primary 3 Basic Science! We observe, measure, and explore the physical world around us.
curriculum.previousKnowledge: Pupils know that some objects are tall, long, short, or wide.

concreteVisualAids.title: Traditional Handspan vs Ruler
concreteVisualAids.description: Illustration showing an outstretched palm (handspan) next to a 30cm plastic school ruler.
concreteVisualAids.caption: Handspan vs. 30cm Metric Ruler

concreteVisualAids.title: Measuring Tape & Metre Rule
concreteVisualAids.description: A wooden 1-metre ruler used by teachers and a flexible tailor measuring tape.
concreteVisualAids.caption: Standard Measuring Tools

whiteboardSteps.title: 1. What is Length?
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Good day champions! Today in Basic Science, we study length. Length is how long something is from one end to another end. If you measure the distance from your classroom door to the blackboard, that distance is length!
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
MEANING OF LENGTH

• Length is the distance between two fixed points or edges.
• Examples:
  - Length of your pencil
  - Length of your classroom desk
  - Height of your school flagpole
bulletPoints: Length measures distance: long, short, wide, tall
Everything around us has a measurable length
whiteboardSteps.equationOrHighlight: Length = Distance from Point A to Point B

whiteboardSteps.title: 2. Traditional vs Standard Units
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Long ago before rulers were made, our grandfathers measured using their bodies: handspans, footsteps, and arm lengths! But why is a handspan not accurate? Because a child has a small hand and an adult teacher has a big hand! That is why we now use standard units: centimeters (cm) and meters (m).
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
MEASURING UNITS

1. Traditional (Non-standard):
   • Handspan (from tip of thumb to little finger)
   • Footstep (paces along the floor)
   • Arm length (cubit)
   ⚠️ Problem: Everyone’s body is different!

2. Standard (Metric):
   • Centimetre (cm) for small objects (pencils, books)
   • Metre (m) for larger distances (doors, rooms)
   • 100 cm = 1 Metre
bulletPoints: Standard units give the same measurement anywhere in the world
A 30cm ruler in Lagos is the exact same length as a 30cm ruler in Kano!

practiceProblems.question: Which of these is a traditional (non-standard) unit of measuring length?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Think of what our ancestors used before rulers were invented.
practiceProblems.explanation: A handspan uses the human palm and is a non-standard traditional unit.

practiceProblems.question: How many centimeters (cm) are in 1 meter (m)?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Look at the markings on a 1-meter stick.
practiceProblems.explanation: There are exactly 100 centimeters in 1 meter (100 cm = 1 m).

assessmentQuestions.question: Why do scientists and builders use standard rulers instead of footsteps to measure a room?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Consider what happens when a tall person and a small pupil pace the same room.
options: Because everyone’s footstep size is different, so it gives inaccurate results
Because rulers are cheaper than shoes
Because footsteps can only measure water
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Different people have different foot and hand sizes, making non-standard measurements inconsistent.
assessmentQuestions.hint: Think about whether your shoe is the same size as your parent’s shoe.

assessmentQuestions.question: Which instrument would a tailor use to measure your waist for a new school uniform?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Think about the flexible tool the tailor wraps around you.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: A tailor uses a flexible measuring tape to measure body curves and lengths.
assessmentQuestions.hint: It can bend easily around a person’s body.

assessmentQuestions.question: What is the best standard unit to measure the length of an exercise book?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Is a notebook huge like a football field or small?
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Small objects like exercise books and pens are measured in centimeters (cm).
assessmentQuestions.hint: Look at the numbers on a student desk ruler.

curriculum.subtopic: Understanding the three main tenses
objectives: Understanding the three main tenses

Examples: "I ate yesterday", "She went to school"
Present tense: actions happening now or regularly
Examples: "I eat rice everyday", "He plays football"
Future tense: actions that will happen
Examples: "I will eat salad tomorrow", "We shall visit grandma"

objectives: Read and write whole numbers up to 1,000,000 (One Million) in figures and words

whiteboardSteps.title: 1. The Millions Place Value Chart
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Welcome to Primary 5 Mathematics! As future leaders and scholars, you must handle large figures like town populations and government investments. To read a 7-digit number, we group digits into groups of three called periods: Units Period, Thousands Period, and Millions Period!
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
7-DIGIT PLACE VALUE CHART

[Millions] | [Thousands Period] | [Units Period]
    M      |  HTh   TTh   Th   |   H    T    U
    3      |   4     8     2   |   5    1    9

• Number: 3,482,519
• Read as: Three Million, Four Hundred and Eighty-Two Thousand, Five Hundred and Nineteen
bulletPoints: Group digits in threes starting from the right (Units)
Insert commas between periods for easy reading
Read the number in each period followed by its period name

whiteboardSteps.title: 2. Expanded Notation & Comparison
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: To find the value of a digit, multiply the digit by its place value. In 5,320,410, the digit 5 has a value of 5 x 1,000,000 = 5,000,000! When comparing two large numbers, look at the highest place value from the left first.
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
EXPANDED FORM & COMPARISON

• 5,320,410 = 5,000,000 + 300,000 + 20,000 + 400 + 10

• Comparing:
  4,520,300  vs  4,519,999
  Both have 4 Millions and 5 Hundred Thousands.
  Compare Ten Thousands: 20,000 > 10,000!
  Therefore: 4,520,300 > 4,519,999
bulletPoints: > means greater than
< means less than
= means equal to

practiceProblems.question: In the number 7,458,921, what is the place value of the digit 7?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Look at the 7th column from the right.
practiceProblems.explanation: The digit 7 is in the Millions column (Value = 7,000,000).

practiceProblems.question: Which symbol correctly completes: 1,250,000 ___ 1,249,999?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Compare the thousands: 50 thousands vs 49 thousands.
practiceProblems.explanation: 1,250,000 is greater than 1,249,999 by 1 unit.

assessmentQuestions.question: How is the number 2,050,400 written in words?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Read period by period: Millions, Thousands, Units.
options: Two million, fifty thousand, four hundred
Two million, five hundred thousand, four hundred
Twenty million, five thousand, four hundred
Two hundred and fifty thousand, four hundred
assessmentQuestions.explanation: 2 is in Millions, 050 is fifty thousand, and 400 is four hundred.
assessmentQuestions.hint: Look at the thousands period: 050 means fifty.

assessmentQuestions.question: What is the value of the digit 8 in 6,841,200?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Multiply 8 by its position (Hundred Thousands).
assessmentQuestions.explanation: 8 is in the Hundred Thousands place, so its value is 800,000.
assessmentQuestions.hint: 8 followed by five zeros.

assessmentQuestions.question: Arrange these figures in ascending order (smallest to largest): 3,100,000; 2,900,000; 3,050,000
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Ascending means climbing up from the lowest number.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: 2.9M is smallest, followed by 3.05M, and 3.1M is largest.
assessmentQuestions.hint: Start with 2,900,000 because 2 million is less than 3 million.

whiteboardSteps.title: 1. Numbers up to Billions (10 Digits)
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Bawo ni, scholars! Welcome to Primary 6. Today we step into Billions. One Billion is 1 followed by nine zeros: 1,000,000,000. It is equal to one thousand millions! Let us see how the periods work together.
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
THE 4 PERIODS OF LARGE NUMBERS

[Billions] | [Millions] | [Thousands] | [Units]
    B      |   H  T  U  |   H  T  U   |  H  T  U
    4      |   2  5  0  |   1  8  0   |  6  0  0

• Read as: Four Billion, Two Hundred and Fifty Million, One Hundred and Eighty Thousand, Six Hundred.
bulletPoints: 1 Billion = 1,000,000,000 (10 digits)
Commas separate each 3-digit period
Read each group of three digits just like in Primary 3, then add the period name

whiteboardSteps.title: 2. Rounding Off Numbers & Roman Numerals
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: To round off to the nearest 1,000, look at the Hundreds digit. If it is 5 or more, round UP by adding 1 to the thousands digit. If less than 5, round DOWN. For Roman numerals, remember: I=1, V=5, X=10, L=50, C=100, D=500, M=1000!
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
ROUNDING OFF RULES & ROMAN NUMERALS

• Rounding 4,862 to nearest 100:
  Tens digit is 6 (>=5) -> Round UP to 4,900!

• Rounding 5,420 to nearest 1,000:
  Hundreds digit is 4 (<5) -> Round DOWN to 5,000!

• Roman Numerals Key:
  I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500, M = 1000
  XC = 100 - 10 = 90
  CD = 500 - 100 = 400
bulletPoints: 5 or more -> Round UP
4 or less -> Round DOWN
Subtract when a smaller Roman numeral precedes a larger one (IV = 4, IX = 9)

practiceProblems.question: How many zeros are in the number One Billion when written in standard figures?
practiceProblems.explanation: One Billion has 9 zeros: 1,000,000,000.

practiceProblems.question: What is the Hindu-Arabic value of the Roman numeral MCMLX?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Break it down: M = 1000, CM = 900, LX = 60.
practiceProblems.explanation: M (1000) + CM (900) + LX (60) = 1960 (the year of Nigerian Independence!).

assessmentQuestions.question: Round off 78,542 to the nearest thousand.
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Look at the hundreds digit (5). Does 5 cause a round up or down?
assessmentQuestions.explanation: The hundreds digit is 5, so we round up 78,000 to 79,000.
assessmentQuestions.hint: Whenever the deciding digit is 5 or more, round up.

assessmentQuestions.question: What is the Roman numeral for 450?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: 400 is CD (500 - 100) and 50 is L.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: CD is 400 and L is 50, so 450 is CDL.
assessmentQuestions.hint: Use subtraction principle for 400: C before D.

assessmentQuestions.question: A state government allocated ₦3,540,800,000 for building primary schools. What period is the digit 3 in?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Count the digits from right to left: units, thousands, millions, billions.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: The digit 3 is in the Billions period (3 Billion Naira).
assessmentQuestions.hint: It is the 10th digit from the right.

Name major rivers (River Niger & River Benue) and where they meet (Lokoja confluence)
Describe the two main seasons in Nigeria: Rainy (Wet) and Dry (Harmattan) seasons
Locate key commercial and administrative cities: Abuja (FCT), Lagos, Kano, Port Harcourt, Enugu, and Ibadan
curriculum.lastWeekRevision: Last week we studied the physical features of our local government area, including hills, valleys, and local water streams.
curriculum.previousKnowledge: Pupils already know Nigeria has 36 states plus the Federal Capital Territory (Abuja) and have observed rainy and dry weather in their hometowns.

concreteVisualAids.title: Geopolitical Map of Nigeria
concreteVisualAids.description: Map showing North-Central, North-East, North-West, South-East, South-South, and South-West zones.
concreteVisualAids.caption: Nigeria with 6 Zones & 36 States

concreteVisualAids.title: The Y-Shaped River Confluence at Lokoja
concreteVisualAids.description: Where River Niger from Guinea highlands joins River Benue from Cameroon mountains to form the Y-shape.
concreteVisualAids.caption: Lokoja River Confluence

whiteboardSteps.title: 1. The 6 Geopolitical Zones of Nigeria
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Look at our country’s map. To govern and organize effectively, Nigeria is grouped into six geopolitical zones: North-West, North-East, North-Central, South-West, South-East, and South-South.
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
NIGERIA’S 6 GEOPOLITICAL ZONES

1. North-West (e.g. Kano, Kaduna, Sokoto)
2. North-East (e.g. Borno, Bauchi, Adamawa)
3. North-Central / Middle Belt (e.g. Plateau, Benue, Niger, FCT Abuja)
4. South-West (e.g. Lagos, Oyo, Ogun, Ondo)
5. South-East (e.g. Enugu, Anambra, Imo, Abia)
6. South-South / Niger Delta (e.g. Rivers, Delta, Akwa Ibom)
bulletPoints: 36 States + 1 Federal Capital Territory (Abuja)
Abuja is in North-Central and is the administrative capital
Lagos is in South-West and is the commercial nerve center

whiteboardSteps.title: 2. Major Rivers: Niger and Benue
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Two great rivers flow through Nigeria like arteries in the human body: River Niger (the longest) and River Benue. They meet at a historic junction called Lokoja in Kogi State. This meeting point forms a giant letter "Y" on the map!
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
THE GREAT RIVERS & CONFLUENCE

• River Niger: Enters from the North-West
• River Benue: Enters from Cameroon in the East
• Confluence City: LOKOJA (Kogi State)
• Flows South into: Atlantic Ocean through the Niger Delta Mangroves
bulletPoints: Confluence = Meeting point of two rivers
Kogi State is nicknamed "The Confluence State"
Provides fresh fish, fertile farmland, and water transportation
whiteboardSteps.equationOrHighlight: River Niger + River Benue = Lokoja Confluence (Y-Shape)

whiteboardSteps.title: 3. Climate and Two Main Seasons in Nigeria
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Unlike Europe where they have four seasons with winter snow, Nigeria experiences a tropical climate with two distinct seasons: The Rainy (Wet) Season and the Dry Season, which brings the cool, dusty Harmattan wind from the Sahara Desert.
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
OUR TWO SEASONS IN NIGERIA

🌧️ RAINY SEASON (April – October):
• Heavy rainfall, lush green vegetation
• Farmers plant yams, maize, cassava

☀️ DRY SEASON (November – March):
• High sunshine and warm days
• Harmattan wind (cool, dry, dusty breeze from the North)
bulletPoints: Southern coastal areas receive more rainfall
Northern savanna areas have longer dry seasons and sunny days
Harmattan brings dry skin and morning mist

practiceProblems.question: At which Nigerian city do River Niger and River Benue meet to form a famous confluence?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Think of the state with the slogan "The Confluence State".
practiceProblems.explanation: River Niger and River Benue meet at Lokoja in Kogi State.

practiceProblems.question: Which geopolitical zone is home to the Federal Capital Territory (Abuja)?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Abuja is located right near the center of Nigeria.
practiceProblems.explanation: Abuja is located in the North-Central geopolitical zone (also known as the Middle Belt).

assessmentQuestions.question: Which of the following states is correctly matched with its geopolitical zone?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Consider the regional grouping of Nigerian states.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Rivers State (Port Harcourt) is in the South-South (Niger Delta) zone.
assessmentQuestions.hint: Rivers State is in the coastal oil-rich delta region of southern Nigeria.

assessmentQuestions.question: During which period of the year does Nigeria typically experience the dry Harmattan season?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Think about when dust from the Sahara and cool mornings occur around Christmas.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: The dry season and Harmattan wind blow between November and March.
assessmentQuestions.hint: It occurs during the dry months when skies are hazy and morning air is brisk.

assessmentQuestions.question: What letter does the confluence of River Niger and River Benue resemble on the map of Nigeria?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Look closely at how the two rivers flow from northwest and east down to the Atlantic.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: The two rivers meet at Lokoja and flow south together, forming the shape of a giant "Y".
assessmentQuestions.hint: It has two branches at the top merging into one stem below.

assessmentQuestions.question: Which city serves as the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) of Nigeria, located in the North-Central zone?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Remember where the seat of the Nigerian federal government is situated.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Abuja is the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) of Nigeria, located in the North-Central geopolitical zone.
assessmentQuestions.hint: It was created to be near the geographic center of the country.

curriculum.contentOutline: Major Nigerian geopolitical zones, rivers Niger and Benue, seasonal climate variations.
learningActivities: Locating zones on Nigerian map
Tracing River Niger and Benue meeting point at Lokoja

curriculum.subject: Mathematics
curriculum.topic: Whole Numbers & Place Value up to 100,000
curriculum.subtopic: Writing in Figures, Words & Expanded Notation
curriculum.periodTitle: Instructional Week 1 · Number & Numeration (Foundation Free Preview)
objectives: Count and write whole numbers up to 100,000 in figures and words
Identify the place value of any digit (Units, Tens, Hundreds, Thousands, Ten Thousands)
Expand numbers using place value decomposition (e.g. 48,250 = 40,000 + 8,000 + 200 + 50)
Solve real-world Nigerian money word problems involving Naira counting
curriculum.lastWeekRevision: In Primary 3, we mastered counting and place value up to 10,000 with cowries and base-10 blocks.
curriculum.previousKnowledge: Pupils know that 10 tens make 100, and 10 hundreds make 1,000, and can count ₦1000 notes.

concreteVisualAids.title: Naira Currency Bundle Chart
concreteVisualAids.description: Bundles of ₦1,000, ₦500, and ₦100 notes demonstrating place value.
concreteVisualAids.caption: 10 x ₦1,000 = ₦10,000 (Ten Thousand)

concreteVisualAids.title: Place Value Abacus Chart
concreteVisualAids.description: 5-spike abacus with beads for Units (U), Tens (T), Hundreds (H), Thousands (Th), and Ten Thousands (T.Th).
concreteVisualAids.caption: Place Value Columns: T.Th | Th | H | T | U

whiteboardSteps.title: 1. Understanding Place Value Columns
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Look at the number 54,321. Every digit has a house where it lives. From right to left: Units (1), Tens (10), Hundreds (100), Thousands (1,000), and Ten Thousands (10,000).
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
PLACE VALUE CHART:

[Ten Thousands] [Thousands] [Hundreds] [Tens] [Units]
       5              4          3        2       1

• 5 Ten Thousands = 50,000
• 4 Thousands     =  4,000
• 3 Hundreds      =    300
• 2 Tens          =     20
• 1 Unit          =      1
Total = Fifty-four thousand, three hundred and twenty-one.
bulletPoints: Always read digits in groups of three from right with a comma
54,321 has 5 Ten Thousands and 4 Thousands
Value of digit 4 is 4,000

whiteboardSteps.title: 2. Expanded Form with Nigerian Market Examples
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Imagine Mama Chidi sold 73,450 Naira worth of yams at Mile 12 Market. Let us break down this money: 70,000 + 3,000 + 400 + 50 + 0.
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
EXPANDED NOTATION:

₦73,450 =
7 Ten Thousands  (₦70,000)
+ 3 Thousands    (₦3,000)
+ 4 Hundreds     (₦400)
+ 5 Tens         (₦50)
+ 0 Units        (₦0)

Word Form: Seventy-three thousand, four hundred and fifty Naira.
bulletPoints: Zero in units column means no single Naira coins
Expanded form shows the true worth of each digit
In words, use hyphen for two-word numbers (seventy-three)

practiceProblems.question: What is the place value of the digit 7 in the number 87,412?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Look at which column 7 sits in: T.Th, Th, H, T, or U.
practiceProblems.explanation: In 87,412, the digit 7 is in the Thousands column (worth 7,000).

practiceProblems.question: How do you write Sixty-five thousand and twenty in figures?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Remember to place a zero in the Hundreds column!
practiceProblems.explanation: Sixty-five thousand and twenty is written as 65,020.

assessmentQuestions.question: In the number 94,832, what is the value of the digit 9?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Look at the highest column on the abacus.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Digit 9 sits in the Ten Thousands column, so its value is 90,000.
assessmentQuestions.hint: It is 9 times 10,000.

assessmentQuestions.question: What is the expanded form of 42,608?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Notice there is a 0 in the Tens column.
assessmentQuestions.hint: Break each digit into its place value.

assessmentQuestions.question: How is the number 75,040 correctly written in words?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Look at each place value group carefully.
options: Seven thousand five hundred and forty
Seven hundred and fifty thousand and forty
assessmentQuestions.explanation: 75 in the thousands group is seventy-five thousand, and 40 in tens is forty: Seventy-five thousand and forty.
assessmentQuestions.hint: Notice the zero in the hundreds column.

assessmentQuestions.question: A trader at Bodija market in Ibadan sold ₦50,000 worth of yams and ₦8,000 worth of plantains. How much money did she make in total?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Add the two amounts using place value columns.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: ₦50,000 + ₦8,000 = ₦58,000 (Fifty-eight thousand Naira).
assessmentQuestions.hint: Add 5 Ten Thousands and 8 Thousands.

curriculum.contentOutline: Place value concepts up to 100,000 using Nigerian currency and concrete counters.
learningActivities: Grouping currency bundles into tens, hundreds, thousands
Abacus exercises

curriculum.subject: Mathematics
curriculum.topic: Fractions: Proper, Improper & Mixed Numbers
curriculum.subtopic: Concrete Visual Slices (Agege Bread & Oranges)
objectives: Identify the numerator (parts taken) and denominator (total equal parts)
Differentiate between Proper Fractions (3/4), Improper Fractions (5/3), and Mixed Numbers (1 2/3)
Convert improper fractions to mixed numbers using real-life food sharing
Compare like and unlike fractions visually
curriculum.lastWeekRevision: Last week we practiced whole numbers up to 100,000.
curriculum.previousKnowledge: Pupils know that sharing a whole orange into 2 equal halves gives 1/2 each, and 4 quarters gives 1/4 each.

concreteVisualAids.title: Loaf of Fresh Agege Bread
concreteVisualAids.description: A whole loaf sliced into 4 equal slices. 3 slices taken = 3/4.
concreteVisualAids.caption: 1 Whole Loaf = 4 Equal Slices (4/4)

concreteVisualAids.title: Sweet Nigerian Oranges
concreteVisualAids.description: Juicy oranges cut into 8 equal segments for sharing among siblings.
concreteVisualAids.caption: Fraction = Part / Whole

whiteboardSteps.title: 1. What is a Fraction?
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: Nno nwam! When you buy a warm loaf of Agege bread from the bakery and slice it into 4 equal pieces, each piece is 1 part out of 4, written as 1/4.
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
ANATOMY OF A FRACTION:

   3  ← NUMERATOR (How many slices we have)
  --- 
   4  ← DENOMINATOR (Total equal slices in 1 whole loaf)

• Top Number (Numerator) = Parts taken
• Bottom Number (Denominator) = Total equal parts
bulletPoints: Denominator CANNOT be zero
Equal parts is mandatory (if slices are uneven, it is not a true fraction!)
4/4 = 1 whole loaf

whiteboardSteps.title: 2. The Three Types of Fractions
whiteboardSteps.teacherSpeech: There are 3 main types: Proper Fractions (small top), Improper Fractions (big heavy top), and Mixed Numbers (a whole number standing next to a fraction).
whiteboardSteps.boardText:
TYPES OF FRACTIONS:

1. PROPER FRACTION: Numerator < Denominator
   Example: 2/5, 3/4, 7/10 (Less than 1 whole)

2. IMPROPER FRACTION: Numerator ≥ Denominator
   Example: 5/3, 9/4 (Greater than 1 whole)

3. MIXED NUMBER: Whole Number + Proper Fraction
   Example: 1 2/3 (1 whole loaf + 2 extra slices)
bulletPoints: 5/3 means you have 5 slices, but 1 whole only takes 3 slices
So 5/3 is the exact same as 1 whole loaf and 2/3 of another loaf (1 2/3)

practiceProblems.question: Which of the following is an IMPROPER fraction?
practiceProblems.concreteContext: Look for the fraction where the top number (numerator) is bigger than the bottom.
practiceProblems.explanation: 9/5 has a numerator (9) larger than denominator (5), making it an improper fraction.

practiceProblems.question: Convert 7/3 into a mixed number.
practiceProblems.concreteContext: How many groups of 3 can you make out of 7? What is the remainder?
practiceProblems.explanation: 7 ÷ 3 = 2 with a remainder of 1. So 7/3 = 2 1/3.

assessmentQuestions.question: In a basket of 10 mangoes, Tunde ate 3 mangoes. What fraction of the mangoes did Tunde eat?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Count the parts taken over the total mangoes in the basket.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: Tunde took 3 mangoes out of 10 total, which is 3/10.
assessmentQuestions.hint: Numerator is 3, Denominator is 10.

assessmentQuestions.question: Which fraction is equivalent to 1/2?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Think of cutting an orange into 4 pieces and taking 2 pieces.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: 2/4 reduces to 1/2 by dividing both top and bottom by 2.
assessmentQuestions.hint: 2 slices out of 4 is half the loaf.

assessmentQuestions.question: Which of the following is an IMPROPER fraction?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Look for a top-heavy fraction where the numerator is greater than the denominator.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: In 7/4, the numerator (7) is greater than the denominator (4), making it an improper fraction.
assessmentQuestions.hint: The top number is larger than the bottom number.

assessmentQuestions.question: If you have 7 slices of Agege bread and 4 slices make 1 whole loaf, what is 7/4 written as a mixed number?
assessmentQuestions.contextNigerian: Count how many full loaves you can make and what fraction remains.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: 7 slices ÷ 4 slices per loaf = 1 whole loaf with 3 slices left over, which is 1 3/4 loaves.
assessmentQuestions.hint: 4 slices make 1 whole loaf, leaving 3 slices out of 4.

curriculum.contentOutline: Proper, improper and mixed fractions using Agege bread and agricultural produce.
learningActivities: Dividing Agege bread loaves into equal slices
Converting mixed numbers to improper fractions
